passage: I'm Vishal, Rajni's neighbour on the third floor. Her son Bittu is four. Whenever anyone speaks to him in the lift, Rajni answers first: "He's the shy one, he won't talk." Yesterday the watchman asked Bittu his name. Bittu opened his mouth, and Rajni said, "Bittu. Sorry, he's very shy." Bittu closed his mouth and hid behind her dupatta. At the building's Holi party, she kept him on her lap instead of letting him join the water-balloon game, saying he'd hate it. Yet I've seen Bittu chatter to my dog through the balcony railing for ten minutes straight. I don't know what goes on in either of their heads. But I wonder if he's learning that his voice isn't needed.

qa.q: How might being called "the shy one" feel to Bittu over time?
qa.a: He might start to believe his voice isn't needed and hide more, even though he clearly chatters away when nobody is labelling him.

passage: Anand, you keep telling people little Meenu is "the shy one." Your old father Tarun has made that mistake before, so listen. When I was twenty-five and your sister Sunita was three, I decided the same about her. At every wedding I answered for her: "Sunita doesn't dance, she's shy." When the school wanted her in the annual-day play, I said no before she could speak. And she became exactly what I said: quiet, always behind a pillar. Then your mother went to her village for a month, and I was alone with Sunita. With nobody speaking for her, she ordered at the sweet shop, argued with the milkman, sang in the bath. I had been building her a small room and calling it her nature. Today Sunita teaches a class of forty. Give Meenu some room.

qa.q: What did young Tarun say at weddings about Sunita?
qa.a: "Sunita doesn't dance, she's shy."

qa.q: What did Tarun realise during the month alone with Sunita?
qa.a: He realised that by answering for her he had been "building her a small room" and calling it her nature, since without him speaking for her she ordered, argued and sang.

qa.q: What choice is Tarun asking Anand to make now?
qa.a: To stop calling Meenu "the shy one" and give her room to speak and try things herself, instead of answering for her.

qa.q: How might Sunita have experienced being "the shy one" as a child?
qa.a: Her father kept speaking and refusing for her, so she may have felt there was no space to try, and quietly became the girl behind the pillar.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a young father sure his daughter was shy, he answered for her and she adopted the role until she was given room.

passage: The overnight train to Kochi was packed and noisy, and Thomas, twenty-six, had his five-year-old son Chinmay tucked beside him on the lower berth. Across the aisle, three children were playing snap. 'Want to play?' a girl called. 'He doesn't like joining in,' Thomas said. Then his office phone rang, and it was his boss, and the connection kept dropping. He went to the door end of the coach to hear. It took twenty minutes. When he came back, Chinmay was sitting cross-legged in the middle of the other berth, slapping cards down. 'I'm Chinmay! I won two!' Thomas stood in the aisle holding his phone, suddenly unsure which of them had been shy.

Binita, you asked how Sehaj got so chatty. I'm Amandeep, and I'll be honest, it was me who had to change, not her.
From when she was two, I told everyone, "She's the shy one." Aunties asked her name, I answered. The shopkeeper offered her a toffee, I said "thank you" for her. At birthday parties, I kept her on my lap so she wouldn't have to join the games.
By four, she'd hide behind my legs and whisper, "I'm shy, Papa, you say it."
Then her teacher told me Sehaj had asked another child to play. I was stunned. So I tried waiting. When the shopkeeper spoke, I just stood there. It took her forever. Then she said, "Thank you, uncle." Tiny voice. But hers.

qa.a: Sehaj may have felt protected but also small, learning that she was the one who couldn't speak.

Vidya, you're a new mother now, so let me tell you something about your uncle Ravi. Come, drink your tea.
When I was twenty-five, Ravi was four, and I was certain he was shy. I said it everywhere: "He's shy, he won't talk." At the doctor's, I answered for him. At school I asked the teacher not to make him stand up.
One day his class had a play. The teacher, Madhuri, came to our door. "Let him be a tree, at least. Trees don't speak." I nearly said no. Then I thought: what if I'm wrong about him?
He was the tree. The next year he was the shopkeeper, with two lines. Now he argues cases in court. I had been so sure. My certainty was the thing keeping him quiet.

qa.q: What role did Ravi play the first year?
qa.a: He was the tree.

qa.a: The elder felt protective and certain, then a flicker of doubt about whether the shy label was really true.

qa.a: The turning point was deciding to say yes to Madhuri's idea of the tree role instead of shielding Ravi again.

qa.q: How might Madhuri, the teacher, have seen Ravi before the play?
qa.a: Madhuri probably saw a child who could do more if given a small, safe chance, which is why she came to the door.

grounding: A young parent sure a son is shy answers for him and shields him from chances, until letting him try in a play gives him room to grow.

At the colony provision shop in Hyderabad, the shopkeeper leaned over the counter. "What's your name, little one?" Payal answered, "Sudha. She's shy, she won't talk." Sudha, who had been about to say it, closed her mouth.
It was the same at the dentist, at the park, at the school gate: Payal spoke first, softly and lovingly, and Sudha let her. When the school sent a form for the Annual Day poem, Payal ticked "not interested" without asking. "She'll freeze on stage," she told her husband.
That evening Sudha stood in front of the mirror reciting the whole poem, word for word, to her reflection. Payal passed the door and stopped.

Note for Ms D'Souza, class teacher, KG-B

You asked at the meeting why Charu never speaks in circle time. I have watched myself this week, and I think part of it is me. On Monday at the clinic the nurse asked Charu how she was, and I said, 'She's very shy, she won't talk.' Charu looked at the floor. On Wednesday at my sister's house, same thing: I answered every question before Charu could open her mouth. On Thursday I tried keeping quiet. The vegetable seller asked her which mangoes she wanted. A long pause, then she pointed and said, 'That one, the yellow.' So from now on I am trying not to call her shy in front of her. Could you give her a small job in circle time too?

Farida (Charu's mother)

qa.a: She could give Charu a small, clear job in circle time and wait patiently for her to speak, matching what worked at the vegetable stall.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt when her mother kept quiet on Thursday?
qa.a: Charu may have felt unsure during the long pause, then proud to choose the mango herself once someone left space for her.

grounding: Shows a parent who labelled her child shy and answered for her, then noticed the pattern and began expecting the child to speak.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage:
14 Nov, night

Big fight with myself today. Jahnavi's school sent a form for the drama club. I almost wrote 'not interested' without asking her, because Jahnavi is the quiet one, everybody knows that. Then I remembered her at Diwali, explaining to her cousins how rockets work, loud and bossy, twenty minutes nonstop. Quiet with strangers, maybe. Not quiet. So I asked her. She shrugged and said, 'Can I just watch first?' Old me would have said 'see, shy' and ticked no. New me said, 'Watch first, then decide.' She's going on Friday. I'm nervous for her, which is silly. Or maybe I'm nervous that she'll love it and I'll have been wrong for six years. Either way, I'm done filling in her life for her.

Darshan

qa.q: Which club was the school form for?
qa.a: The drama club.

qa.q: What is Darshan nervous about by the end of the entry?
qa.a: Darshan feels nervous and uneasy that Jahnavi will love the club, which would show the 'quiet one' label had been wrong for six years.

qa.q: What went differently from the old habit, and what could Darshan keep doing?
qa.a: Instead of ticking 'not interested', Darshan asked Jahnavi and agreed she could watch first; asking before deciding for her is worth keeping.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see being asked instead of being answered for?
qa.a: Jahnavi may feel trusted and less pressured, since she can watch first and then decide for herself.

grounding: A parent nearly closes a door because the child is 'the quiet one', then asks her and gives her room to grow.
